```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(cloudscape)
set.seed(1)
```

## The question

You want land-surface phenology from optical imagery. Before committing, you
want to know whether the site will yield a defensible green-up date, and if
not, what would change that.

Mean cloud cover cannot answer this. Two sites with the same annual cloud
cover can differ in retrieval error, depending on *when* the cloud falls and
how it clusters in time.

## Step 1: how many observations, and when

```{r}
dates <- seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "5 days")
site <- cl_simulate_series(dates, p_cloud = 0.62, persistence = 0.4, seed = 11)
obs <- cl_obs(cell = 1, date = site$date, cloud_fraction = site$cloud_fraction,
              sensor = "sentinel-2-msi")

cl_stats_wide(cl_gaps(obs, threshold = 0.2, critical = 21))
```

The maximum gap matters more than the count. A 40-day gap that happens to
straddle green-up removes the transition entirely, and no amount of data later
in the season recovers it.

## Step 2: translate into days of error

```{r}
p <- cl_pheno_power(dates, cloud_fraction = site$cloud_fraction,
                    n_sim = 300, seed = 2)
p$summary[, c("n_retained_median", "sos_mae", "sos_iqr", "sos_bias",
              "failure_rate", "p_within_all")]
```

Read the failure rate first. It is the share of replicates in which too few
observations remained, the fit did not converge, or the fitted curve lacked a
start, peak or end of season. A study that fails to produce an estimate is a
different problem from one that produces a biased estimate, and the two get
confused when only the error of successful retrievals is reported.
`p_within_all` combines both: the probability that a retrieval succeeds and
all three dates fall within `tolerance` days (5 by default) of the truth.

## Step 3: how sensitive is this to clustering?

```{r}
grid <- expand.grid(cloud = c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8), tau = c(0, 5, 20))
res <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(cl, tau) {
  s <- cl_pheno_power(dates, cloud_fraction = cl, tau = tau,
                      n_sim = 250, seed = 5)$summary
  data.frame(cloud = cl, tau = tau, retained = s$n_retained_median,
             sos_mae = s$sos_mae, failure = round(s$failure_rate, 3),
             within = round(s$p_within_all, 3))
}, grid$cloud, grid$tau))
res
```

`tau` is the decorrelation time of cloud loss in days. At constant cloud, the
number of retained observations barely changes with `tau`, because every
acquisition keeps its clear probability; what changes is how the losses are
arranged in time. Long decorrelation times remove runs of consecutive
acquisitions, which can take out a whole transition. Estimate `tau` for the
site with `cl_persistence()` rather than assuming it.

## Step 4: would adding a sensor fix it?

```{r}
sy <- cl_synergy(c("landsat-8-9-oli", "sentinel-2-msi"),
                 "2015-01-01", "2025-12-31")
sy[sy$period == "2025", c("sensor", "n_platforms", "combined_obs",
                          "effective_revisit_days")]
```

Adding Landsat to Sentinel-2 shortens the effective revisit. Whether that
converts into usable observations depends on whether the two constellations are
clouded at the same times, so the gain in usable observations can be smaller
than the revisit numbers suggest. Verify with the actual archive rather than
assuming.

## Step 5: state the design explicitly

```{r}
cl_feasibility(p_clear = 0.38, n_acquisitions = 73, n_required = 15,
               window_days = 365, max_gap = 30)
```

## What to report in a paper

State the acquisition count, the maximum gap, and the simulated retrieval error
with its failure rate, for each site or stratum. Reporting mean cloud cover
alone leaves readers unable to judge whether the phenological conclusions are
supportable, and leaves you unable to explain why one site behaved differently
from another.

A caveat worth carrying: everything above uses simulated cloud fractions. With
real data, scene-level cloud cover is a footprint average that says nothing
about where in the scene the cloud was; quality layers read with `cl_qa_obs()`
measure each cell, and the difference between the two tiers is itself
informative.
